title: Burst option discovery + peak traffic patterns (Northpeak Search)
topics: Current production workload and peak patterns (indexing vs query traffic)
Baseline sizing for Dedicated (GPU count, concurrency, headroom)
What “burst” means operationally (temporary capacity, admission control, guardrails)
Denial behavior (queue/backpressure vs immediate 429) and client retry strategy
How to decide between increasing reservation vs using burst
Observability expectations (tenant-visible usage, denials, neighbor impact signals)
Timeline and success criteria for a pilot
summary: Northpeak Search described a steady online query workload plus predictable indexing spikes (2–3x baseline) tied to weekly re-index jobs and occasional product launches. Redwood walked through how Dedicated baseline reservations should be sized to protect p95 latency during normal traffic, and how a paid Burst option can cover short windows of additional throughput without permanently increasing reserved GPUs. The group discussed guardrails: per-tenant burst caps/ratios, cooldowns, fleet safety limits, and how burst denials surface (429 vs backpressure) with deterministic reason codes. Next steps: Northpeak to share a 7-day traffic shape and indexing job schedule; Redwood to propose baseline + burst caps for us-east (H100/L40S options) and send a pilot plan with observability and billing assumptions.
questions: If we burst during indexing, can it impact our own online query SLOs (same tenant) and how do we isolate those routes?
What does a burst denial look like in the API—immediate 429, queued, or partial completion?
How do you meter burst—GPU-seconds vs tokens—and how do retries avoid double counting?
Can we pre-schedule burst windows or is it purely reactive to load?
Is burst restricted to a region/hardware class and what happens if that pool is saturated?
action_items: Northpeak (Amit/Lena): Send Redwood a 7-day view of request rate + token distribution (p50/p95 input/output tokens) split by 'query' vs 'index' routes.
Northpeak (Tom): Confirm target region(s) for first phase (likely us-east) and any data residency constraints.
Redwood (Simran): Draft sizing recommendation: baseline reserved GPUs + suggested max burst ratio/cap and cooldown defaults for indexing spikes.
Redwood (Stephanie): Share pilot proposal email with success criteria (throughput during index job, p95 for query route, denial rate target) and rough pricing ranges for burst add-on.
Redwood (Simran): Send doc link on denial reason codes + recommended client retry/backoff behavior.
next_steps: Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive on routing separation (query vs index) and backpressure strategy next week.
Redwood to provide a baseline+burst configuration proposal once Northpeak shares traffic shapes.
If proposal looks good, identify 1–2 weeks for a Dedicated pilot with burst enabled and load test windows.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-02-13
Start time: 6:30 PM PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Title: Burst option discovery + peak traffic patterns (Northpeak Search)
Organizer: Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood Inference)
Attendees (Redwood): Stephanie Nguyen (AE), Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect)
Attendees (Northpeak): Amit Desai (Platform Eng Lead), Lena Hoffman (ML Eng), Tom Alvarez (SRE/Infra)

Auto-generated summary
- Customer has steady query traffic and predictable weekly indexing spikes.
- They want a Dedicated baseline that protects query latency, and burst capacity for indexing jobs.
- Discussed how burst is admitted/denied and what observability + billing would look like.


[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. This one is mostly discovery—peak patterns, how you size today, and then we can talk about when burst makes sense versus just reserving more GPUs.

[00:15] Amit Desai: Yep. We’re evaluating Dedicated because our current setup is… kind of stitched together.

[00:21] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. Simran’s here too, she can go deep on the technical side. Maybe quick intros?

[00:28] Simran Kaur: Hey all, Simran, solutions architect. I work with folks on sizing, routing, and the “what happens when it’s overloaded” bits.

[00:37] Lena Hoffman: Lena, ML engineer. I own the retrieval + reranking model serving side.

[00:43] Tom Alvarez: Tom, SRE/infra. I mostly care about not waking up at 3 AM.

[00:48] Stephanie Nguyen: The best job. Amit, do you want to give the 2-minute overview of workload and why now?

[01:00] Amit Desai: Sure. We’re a search company—customer support search, internal knowledge base. We run an embeddings pipeline and then a reranker at query time. The pain is we have two very different traffic shapes. Query is pretty steady, but indexing is like a weekly… storm.

[01:17] Stephanie Nguyen: Weekly storm, love that.

[01:19] Amit Desai: Every Sunday night we re-index a bunch of tenant corpuses, and we run heavier LLM steps then. That job tries to finish before Monday morning, but sometimes it bleeds into business hours.

[01:32] Simran Kaur: Is the indexing job using the same model endpoint as query-time rerank, or different?

[01:38] Lena Hoffman: Different endpoints. Query-time rerank is smaller, lower latency. Indexing uses a larger model plus some extraction and summarization. Not like full chat, but still generation.

[01:52] Simran Kaur: Got it. So you already separate the routes, that’s good.

[01:56] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we quantify “steady” versus “storm”? Like baseline QPS, token sizes, what does the spike look like.

[02:07] Amit Desai: For query-time rerank, we’re around 120 requests per second at peak weekdays. It’s not crazy, but it’s continuous. For indexing, it’s batchy—we’ll spin up workers and it can 3x or 4x the GPU demand.

[02:23] Tom Alvarez: It’s less QPS and more concurrency, right? Each job is long-ish.

[02:27] Lena Hoffman: Yeah, indexing calls are longer contexts. Inputs can be 3k tokens, outputs maybe 500-ish, depending. Query-time is like 300 in, 50 out.

[02:41] Simran Kaur: Okay that’s important because the long-context stuff eats KV cache and you’ll see throughput swing depending on sequence length distribution.

[02:49] Stephanie Nguyen: When you say 3–4x demand, is it 3–4x for like an hour, or is it like a whole day?

[02:56] Amit Desai: Usually 6 to 10 hours. Sundays are the big one. Then we have smaller spikes when a big customer imports a new dataset, or after a product launch.

[03:09] Stephanie Nguyen: So predictable-ish: weekly plus occasional events.

[03:13] Amit Desai: Exactly.

[03:15] Simran Kaur: What are you running on today? Like, self-hosted, managed endpoints, multiple vendors?

[03:22] Amit Desai: AWS mostly. We have a mix: some on SageMaker endpoints for the rerank, and then for generation we’ve tried Together and a bit of Modal. It’s not consistent.

[03:34] Tom Alvarez: And costs are… not stable. Every time we overprovision for indexing, we pay for it all week.

[03:41] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s the classic “paying rent for the holiday party” problem.

[03:45] Lena Hoffman: Plus, we see latency tail issues when indexing overlaps with query.

[03:50] Simran Kaur: Tail latency where? In your query endpoint or across everything?

[03:54] Lena Hoffman: Query endpoint. Even though separate routes, they share some infra. So when indexing runs, we start seeing p95 go from, say, 250ms to 600ms.

[04:06] Simran Kaur: Got it. That’s basically the noisy neighbor scenario, even if it’s “your own neighbor.” In Dedicated, the first principle is: baseline capacity sized for the always-on workload, and then bursts should not be allowed to eat that baseline in a way that breaks the SLO you care about.

[04:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Right, and from our side, burst is an add-on that lets you exceed your reserved baseline temporarily by borrowing from a managed pool, but with guardrails so it doesn’t blow up other tenants or the fleet.

[04:34] Tom Alvarez: When you say “borrowing,” what happens if the pool is empty? Like, it’s first come first serve?

[04:41] Simran Kaur: Not purely. There’s admission control. You can think of it as: request comes in tagged as eligible to burst—based on route policy and tenant config—and then the admission controller checks: are you under your burst cap, is the pool under safety thresholds, and are you within fairness constraints. If yes, you get admitted, routed to burst capacity. If not, you get denied with a reason.

[05:04] Amit Desai: Denied meaning 429?

[05:06] Simran Kaur: Often 429 or “overloaded” depending on the gateway behavior. We can also do backpressure/queue for certain routes, but that’s something we’d design intentionally. For indexing batch jobs, queuing might be acceptable. For interactive query, usually you want immediate fail fast and retry to a smaller model or a fallback.

[05:27] Lena Hoffman: We could queue indexing, yeah. It’s not user-facing.

[05:31] Stephanie Nguyen: One thing we want to avoid is you thinking burst is infinite. It’s basically insurance for peaks, but it’s bounded and observable.

[05:42] Amit Desai: Makes sense. So how do we decide baseline vs burst? Like, if our Sunday job is 6–10 hours, is that “burst” or should we reserve more?

[05:54] Simran Kaur: Great question. The rule of thumb: if you’re above baseline for a large fraction of the week, it’s cheaper and more reliable to raise the reservation. If it’s a short window—like single-digit hours, once a week—burst can be cost-effective.

[06:11] Tom Alvarez: Single digit, but it’s every week.

[06:13] Simran Kaur: Right—so we’d look at utilization. If it’s 10 hours out of 168 hours, that’s ~6%. That’s a good burst candidate.

[06:23] Stephanie Nguyen: And the baseline reservation then is sized for weekday steady + some headroom for jitter.

[06:28] Lena Hoffman: Our fear is the overlap. If Sunday job bleeds into Monday, we can’t have query degrade.

[06:35] Simran Kaur: Yep. We can enforce per-route burst eligibility. For example, “indexing route can burst up to X, query route cannot burst and is protected.” Then, even within your tenant, we can prevent indexing from consuming the baseline budget that query uses.

[06:54] Amit Desai: Is that like separate deployments?

[06:56] Simran Kaur: It can be separate model deployments or separate capacity partitions behind the same Dedicated cluster. Practically, you’d have two logical services with quotas. We’d propose an architecture after we see your traffic split.

[07:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Can you share rough numbers on indexing throughput requirement? Like, “we need to process N docs by Monday.”

[07:17] Lena Hoffman: Yes. We have a hard-ish deadline: finish 20 million docs reprocessing in 8 hours for the big run. But it’s not always 20 million; it varies.

[07:30] Simran Kaur: And per doc, are you doing one generation call, or multiple passes?

[07:34] Lena Hoffman: Usually one extraction summary, sometimes two if quality check fails. Also embeddings, but that’s separate.

[07:44] Simran Kaur: Ok. So for sizing, we’d want: (1) distribution of input/output tokens for that route, (2) target completion time, (3) concurrency you can drive.

[07:57] Tom Alvarez: We can drive a lot of concurrency, but we learned the hard way it just creates a thundering herd.

[08:04] Simran Kaur: Yeah, and that’s where admission control + client-side rate limits matter.

[08:09] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s dig into your peak patterns. Do you have a daily curve? Like, query traffic is steady, but is there a lunch peak, weekdays vs weekends?

[08:20] Amit Desai: Weekdays are higher. It’s mostly US business hours. We see a 2x peak around 10 AM to 2 PM Pacific.

[08:30] Simran Kaur: Region wise, are you mostly us-west or us-east today?

[08:34] Tom Alvarez: us-east-1 mostly, because customers are mixed and our data plane is there.

[08:39] Simran Kaur: Great, that aligns with our initial burst pools. Early support is region-scoped, so you’d burst within us-east for a given hardware class.

[08:49] Amit Desai: Hardware class meaning H100 vs L40S?

[08:52] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[08:54] Stephanie Nguyen: For some customers, rerank goes on L40S, generation on H100, depending on model and latency.

[09:01] Lena Hoffman: We care more about consistent throughput than the absolute fastest p50.

[09:06] Simran Kaur: Good. That tends to favor dedicated baseline with some batching.

[09:12] Tom Alvarez: What are the actual guardrails for burst? Like, could we burst 5x?

[09:17] Simran Kaur: Typically no, not by default. There’s a max burst ratio and a cap—both per-tenant and per pool. Exact numbers depend on pool health and contract tier. The goal is: you can temporarily exceed baseline, but not in a way that destabilizes others.

[09:36] Stephanie Nguyen: And there are cooldown windows too—so you don’t do “burst, drop, burst, drop” every 30 seconds.

[09:44] Amit Desai: That would be us.

[09:46] (crosstalk)

[09:48] Lena Hoffman: For indexing, I’d rather have a smooth extra 2x for a few hours than spiky 5x anyway.

[09:55] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Smooth is easier on the system and usually cheaper.

[10:01] Stephanie Nguyen: On pricing, I’m not going to quote exact numbers on this call, but conceptually: you pay for the reserved baseline monthly, and burst is metered based on actual usage during burst windows.

[10:13] Tom Alvarez: Metered how? GPU-hours?

[10:16] Simran Kaur: Under the hood, we can measure GPU-seconds attributable to burst, plus tokens processed. For customer reporting, we typically map it to a clear “burst usage” line item. Also, retries are tricky—so we use idempotency keys to avoid double counting. That’s something we’ve been hardening.

[10:37] Amit Desai: Ok.

[10:38] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to make sure we capture what success looks like. Is it: Sunday job finishes by Monday, and query p95 stays under X even if indexing overlaps?

[10:49] Lena Hoffman: Yes. Query p95 under 300ms is our internal goal. Indexing can be slower.

[10:56] Tom Alvarez: And fewer “mystery throttles.” Today we get throttled but don’t know why.

[11:03] Simran Kaur: Denial reason codes are a big part of the burst design. You’ll see things like: “tenant cap reached,” “pool saturated,” “cooldown active,” or “fleet safety gate.” Not those exact strings, but that concept.

[11:19] Amit Desai: Fleet safety gate sounds ominous.

[11:21] Simran Kaur: It’s basically: if the platform detects risk to non-burst SLOs, it shuts the door. That’s how we protect neighbors.

[11:30] Stephanie Nguyen: It’s also how we protect you from a bad day becoming an incident.

[11:35] Tom Alvarez: How do you detect “risk”? Is it latency-based?

[11:39] Simran Kaur: Several signals: pool saturation, queue depth, telemetry lag, and tail latency deltas for non-burst traffic. The idea is that if non-burst p95 starts regressing beyond thresholds, burst gets reduced or disabled.

[11:58] Lena Hoffman: So burst can be disabled dynamically?

[12:01] Simran Kaur: Yes, via circuit breakers. And it’s auditable.

[12:06] Tom Alvarez: Auditable like audit logs?

[12:08] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Config changes, overrides, things like that.

[12:13] Stephanie Nguyen: We can follow up with security docs if you need them, but I know today is more capacity planning.

[12:20] Amit Desai: Staying on sizing: if our baseline is, say, 8 GPUs, and burst gives us 4 more during Sunday, is that a typical shape?

[12:30] Simran Kaur: It can be. But I’d rather anchor on throughput. For query, we’ll size so that at weekday peaks you’re not at 95% utilization. Like, maybe 60–70% at peak to keep tail stable.

[12:45] Lena Hoffman: That’s what we don’t do today.

[12:47] Simran Kaur: Most people don’t.

[12:50] Stephanie Nguyen: Could you share, even if rough, current spend and what you’re trying to optimize—cost vs latency vs predictability?

[12:59] Amit Desai: Predictability. We’re okay paying more than “spot,” we just can’t have it fluctuate 2x month to month.

[13:09] Tom Alvarez: Also we don’t want to constantly change instance counts.

[13:12] Stephanie Nguyen: That fits Dedicated.

[13:15] Simran Kaur: One more important question: when indexing runs, do you run it at full speed no matter what, or can you slow it down based on backpressure?

[13:25] Lena Hoffman: We can slow it down. We control the worker pool.

[13:28] Simran Kaur: Great. Then you can treat burst as “available when admitted,” and otherwise you throttle the workers.

[13:36] Tom Alvarez: If the burst pool is saturated, do we just get 429s?

[13:40] Simran Kaur: Either 429 or a structured denial. For batch routes, we can optionally support queued admission, but you still need to handle it gracefully.

[13:51] Amit Desai: I’d prefer not to add queue complexity unless we have to.

[13:55] Simran Kaur: Totally fair. Simple approach: if you get a denial reason “pool saturated,” you back off with jitter. If it’s “tenant cap,” you know you’ve hit your configured limit and the only fix is lowering demand or raising cap.

[14:11] Stephanie Nguyen: We can share recommended retry behavior. We’ve seen customers accidentally DDoS themselves with aggressive retries.

[14:19] Lena Hoffman: Guilty.

[14:21] (crosstalk)

[14:23] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk about those occasional peaks—launches. How often and how big?

[14:29] Amit Desai: Quarterly maybe. When we launch, we have more ingestion, so indexing spikes again. That might be 2 days, not just one night.

[14:39] Simran Kaur: Two days is still “burstable” depending on frequency, but it starts to become a business decision. If it’s quarterly, burst can still make sense.

[14:49] Tom Alvarez: Can we pre-book burst? Like schedule Sunday 8 PM to 4 AM?

[14:54] Simran Kaur: Today, it’s primarily reactive, based on demand and policy. We’re discussing scheduled windows as an enhancement, but I wouldn’t promise it. What we can do is set caps and priorities such that when you request, you’re more likely to be admitted.

[15:11] Stephanie Nguyen: In other words, you can plan for it, but it’s not a hard reservation of the burst pool.

[15:16] Amit Desai: Understood.

[15:18] Simran Kaur: Also, initially it’s within region. So if us-east pool is hot, it won’t automatically spill to us-west.

[15:27] Tom Alvarez: That’s fine. Data is in us-east anyway.

[15:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Can we quickly cover model requirements? Are you tied to a specific open model?

[15:37] Lena Hoffman: We’re using a fine-tuned Llama variant for extraction. For rerank, it’s a smaller cross-encoder. We can be flexible as long as quality stays.

[15:49] Simran Kaur: If you can send token distributions, we can simulate throughput on H100 vs L40S. For long context extraction, H100 tends to be more forgiving.

[16:02] Amit Desai: Ok.

[16:03] Stephanie Nguyen: Tom, any security constraints that would block a hosted control plane, or you’re okay with Dedicated managed by Redwood?

[16:10] Tom Alvarez: For now, Dedicated is fine. We’ll need audit logs and RBAC eventually, but not VPC-only day one.

[16:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[16:21] Simran Kaur: Back to sizing: do you have metrics today, like p95 input tokens, p95 output tokens for each route?

[16:28] Lena Hoffman: We do, but not cleanly. We can export from our gateway logs.

[16:33] Simran Kaur: Even approximate is fine to start.

[16:36] Amit Desai: We can send a 7-day slice.

[16:39] Stephanie Nguyen: That would be awesome. Also, if you can split query vs index traffic, that helps.

[16:45] Tom Alvarez: We can.

[16:47] Simran Kaur: One more nuance: if indexing uses big contexts, it can increase memory pressure and reduce effective batch sizes. So it’s good you separate routes.

[16:58] Lena Hoffman: Is “burst” compatible with continuous batching? Or does it break that.

[17:03] Simran Kaur: It’s compatible. The burst decision is at admission/routing time, not in the kernel. Once admitted, it’s just GPU capacity. The main thing is the scheduler must be aware so we don’t starve non-burst work.

[17:16] Amit Desai: Okay.

[17:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Can you share what “baseline” looks like today? Like how many GPUs are you keeping warm?

[17:24] Tom Alvarez: For the query rerank, we keep 4 A10s equivalent. For indexing, we spin up to 12 at peak, then back down to 2. That’s on AWS.

[17:37] Simran Kaur: That’s pretty spiky.

[17:39] Tom Alvarez: Exactly.

[17:41] Simran Kaur: In Dedicated, we might suggest something like: baseline sized for query plus minimum indexing trickle, and then burst covers the spike. But we’ll see.

[17:54] Lena Hoffman: If we do Dedicated, can we still scale baseline sometimes? Like monthly change.

[17:59] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, baseline can be resized via contract changes—usually not hourly. Burst is for the hour-to-hour variability.

[18:09] Amit Desai: That’s the piece we want.

[18:12] Tom Alvarez: Operationally, how do we know we’re bursting? Is there a dashboard?

[18:17] Simran Kaur: Yes. You’d see burst usage over time, admitted vs denied requests, and denial reasons. Also pool saturation and any neighbor-impact indicators on our side. Customer-facing views show your own usage and denials.

[18:34] Lena Hoffman: Can we export usage for finance?

[18:36] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, we can provide reports and billing line items. We can talk details later.

[18:43] Tom Alvarez: Ok.

[18:45] (short pause)

[18:47] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to make sure we’re aligned on “when not to use burst.” Simran, can you say it plainly?

[18:54] Simran Kaur: Sure. If you’re bursting all day every day, you should just increase the reservation. Burst is not meant to be your steady-state. Also, if you need a hard guarantee of extra GPUs at a specific time, burst is best-effort within guardrails—not an additional reservation.

[19:14] Amit Desai: That’s helpful.

[19:16] Lena Hoffman: For Sunday, best-effort is okay as long as we can still finish by Monday most of the time.

[19:22] Simran Kaur: Then we’ll tune caps and worker behavior to reach that.

[19:27] Tom Alvarez: And if it’s not enough, we reserve more.

[19:29] Simran Kaur: Exactly.

[19:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Timeline wise, when do you want something live?

[19:36] Amit Desai: Ideally March or April we start pilot. We have a renewal coming mid-year and want to decide before that.

[19:45] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. We can move quickly. Next step is: you send traffic shapes, we send sizing proposal, then do a technical deep dive on routing/backpressure.

[19:58] Lena Hoffman: Works.

[20:00] Tom Alvarez: One more question: if you deny burst, does it ever fall back to baseline automatically? Like, can a request just run slower instead of failing?

[20:10] Simran Kaur: Good question. For some workloads, yes—if your baseline has spare capacity, the request can still be served without burst. Burst is only needed when you exceed baseline. If baseline is saturated and burst is denied, then you need to fail/backoff/queue.

[20:26] Tom Alvarez: So denial doesn’t mean “no service,” it means “no extra.”

[20:29] Simran Kaur: Exactly. Denial is about the incremental capacity.

[20:33] Amit Desai: That clarifies a lot.

[20:36] Stephanie Nguyen: We’re at time, but I want to do a quick recap and assign next steps.

[20:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Northpeak will send us a 7-day traffic profile split by query vs index, token sizes, and your Sunday job schedule. Tom will confirm regions and any constraints. Simran will draft a baseline + burst cap recommendation and send a doc on denial codes and retry guidance. I’ll send a pilot proposal with success criteria and rough pricing bands. Then we’ll schedule a technical deep dive next week.

[21:10] Amit Desai: Sounds good.

[21:12] Lena Hoffman: Yep.

[21:13] Tom Alvarez: Works.

[21:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Great, thanks all.

(Recording ended early by Fireflies; remainder of meeting included calendar scheduling and was not captured.)
